stories.original:
**Canada launches instant payments after years of delays**

*A long-delayed real-time rail is now live, with immediate implications for European banks and payment firms routing cross-border flows to and from Canada.*

After a protracted development process marked by multiple delays, Payments Canada has launched its instant payments network, bringing one of Europe's largest trade and remittance partners into line with the global expectation that domestic payment systems support real-time clearing.

The launch shifts the operational question for European banks and payment service providers with Canadian exposure from readiness to integration. Cross-border corridors between Canada and the euro area or UK stand to benefit as the real-time rail matures and connects to international schemes. More than 80% of Canadian payments destined for Europe are currently routed through correspondent banking channels that the new system is designed to modernise.

Canada's experience mirrors a pattern seen across several G7 economies: political commitment to instant payments followed by lengthy infrastructure build-outs. The UK's Faster Payments launched in 2008, and the euro area's instant credit transfer scheme has been live since 2017, though full adoption under the instant payments regulation only became mandatory in October 2025.

*Sources: [Canada's instant payments network launches after years of delays](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-payments-canada-launches-real-time-rail-system/) — The Globe and Mail*

stories.original:
**ECB urges wider SEPA adoption as costly transfers persist across Europe**

*Despite the instant payments mandate now in force, high-cost transfers remain common in several member states, with Cyprus among those where the central bank wants faster progress.*

The European Central Bank (ECB) has called on banks and consumers to make greater use of Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) transfers, citing persistent reliance on expensive legacy payment methods despite the instant payments regulation requiring banks to offer round-the-clock instant transfers since October 2025. In Cyprus, the proportion of instant transfers among all credit transfers has reached almost 32 per cent by volume, but the ECB regards this as insufficient.

The intervention comes roughly a year after the instant payments regulation took effect. While the regulation mandated that banks receive and send instant payments at no premium to standard transfers, the ECB's concern suggests that behavioural and commercial barriers continue to slow adoption. Banks in some markets have been slow to promote instant payments or to retire higher-cost alternatives.

Payment service providers and fintechs building on euro instant rails face tightening regulatory expectations. The European Commission opened its first enforcement cases under the regulation in June, and continued pressure from the ECB points toward further supervisory attention.

*Sources: [ECB urges greater use of SEPA as costly money transfers persist across Europe](https://cyprus-mail.com/2026/11/09/ecb-urges-greater-use-of-sepa-as-costly-money-transfers-persist-across-europe) — Cyprus-mail | [ECB urges wider use of SEPA amid costly transfers — Cyprus Mail](https://ua.news/en/dovkolo-svitu/etsb-zaklikav-aktivnishe-koristuvatisia-sepa-cherez-dorogi-perekazi-cyprus-mail) — UA.NEWS*

stories.original:
**Industry leaders call for consumer protections before agentic payments scale**

*As AI agents begin initiating live transactions across Europe, senior figures argue that existing frameworks leave gaps in liability, consent and dispute resolution that must be closed before widespread adoption.*

Industry leaders are pressing for clearer consumer protection rules as agentic payments move from pilots to early production. The concern centres on accountability: when an AI agent initiates a payment on a consumer's behalf, existing regulatory frameworks do not clearly assign liability for errors, unauthorised transactions or disputes. Several voices have pointed to commercial variable recurring payments as a potential model, since they allow transactions within customer-authorised parameters.

The call comes after a rapid sequence of live agentic payment transactions across Europe over recent months, involving major card networks, banks and fintechs. While the technical plumbing has advanced quickly, the regulatory and consumer protection architecture has not kept pace. The Financial Conduct Authority announced on October 19 that it would develop a framework for agentic finance alongside industry and other regulators, but binding rules remain some distance away.

Agentic commerce is moving from concept to deployment faster than most industry observers expected. Without clear rules on consent delegation, transaction limits and redress, the risk is that early consumer harm triggers a regulatory backlash that slows adoption more than proactive rulemaking would.

*Sources: [Industry leaders call for clearer consumer protections as agentic payments develop](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/industry-leaders-call-for-clearer-consumer-protections-as-agentic-payments-develop/) — Openbankingexpo*

stories.original:
**UK government drops open banking approach to benefits surveillance**

*A shift to requiring banks to check their own data and report limited information back to government removes the open banking layer from benefits monitoring, but raises fresh questions about consent-based data sharing.*

The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has confirmed it will not use open banking to monitor the bank accounts of benefit claimants, dropping a previous proposal that relied on claimant consent. Under the replacement approach, known as the eligibility verification measure, banks will check their own customer data against specific eligibility indicators set by the DWP and report limited information back to the department. The DWP does not gain direct access to account data; instead, the process bypasses claimant consent by placing the obligation on banks to flag relevant cases.

The original proposal had attracted significant scrutiny from privacy campaigners and parts of the fintech industry, with concerns that using consent-based open banking infrastructure for state surveillance would undermine trust in the broader ecosystem. The DWP's rationale for the change is operational: the consent-based approach could not be applied universally across all Universal Credit claims.

The decision removes the risk that government surveillance becomes associated with open banking rails, but it also demonstrates the limits of consent-based data sharing when the state determines that voluntary participation is insufficient.

*Sources: [Major update on DWP plan to 'snoop' on bank accounts of benefit claimants](https://www.cambridge-news.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/major-update-dwp-plan-snoop-34882585) — Cambridge-news*
